item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies will look to improve a roster that once again dealt with injuries and shortcomings, leading to an early exit in the postseason.
The two corner outfield spots are key areas Dave Dombrowski, Preston Mattingly and the front office will need to focus on, along with the bullpen.
Left field has been a platoon over the last two seasons, while the team has struggled to get typical corner outfield production from a right fielder since Nick Castellanos’ All-Star season in 2023, where he clubbed 29 home runs and drove in a career-best 106 runs.
Since 2021, the Phillies have had 26 different starters in left field, with Brandon Marsh, Kyle Schwarber and Andrew McCutchen getting the majority of the starts during that stretch.
Over in right field, the Phillies also penciled in 26 different names to patrol right field, with Nick Castellanos and Bryce Harper earning the lion's share.
Despite the upcoming free agent pool being quite shallow, Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are a pair of outfielders on the market that the Phillies should target that could provide stability for multiple seasons.
Entering his age 32 season next year (assuming there is a season), Arozarena could be an intriguing pickup for the Phillies. He was named an All-Star with the Seattle Mariners after slashing .281/.381/.484 with an .865 OPS. He hit 26 home runs and drove in 79 runs.
He posted a 151 wRC+ and 5.7 WAR.
Stacking him up to the hitters in the Phillies’ lineup this season, he would have ranked within the top five in AVG, OBP, SLG, OPS, HR and RBIs.
Arozarena is coming off essentially a career year. His triple slash line numbers represent career highs in a full season for the outfielder, and it could have been an outlier campaign for him.
Nonetheless, even his career numbers at .255/.350/.442 and .792 OPS, along with his ability to hit 20-plus homers in six straight seasons, warrant a phone call from the Phillies, who may need him more than any other team in the league.
He would provide much-needed pop from the right side of the plate, something this lineup has been missing for a few years. This season, the Phillies ranked 22nd in MLB in OPS and 28th in on-base percentage from their right-handed hitters.
He also has more speed on the basepaths than Suzuki, adding some athleticism to a Phillies lineup that can become station-to-station at times.
Defensively, he isn't great, but the Phillies need stabilizing bats in the lineup due to the consistent ebbs and flows this lineup has endured over the course of the last handful of seasons, especially come playoff time.
Perhaps the biggest selling point for Arozerena may not be what he does over 162 games, but what he's already done when the stakes are highest.
His postseason résumé gives him an element Suzuki simply doesn't have at the major league level—a proven ability to become a difference-maker when the calendar flips to October.
Arozarena has plenty of experience playing in big moments. He has played in 45 career postseason games, slashing .292/.380/.565 with a .946 OPS across 184 plate appearances. He also has hit 12 bombs in the playoffs and has a knack for the theatrics.
Bringing him in would more than likely mean Brandon Marsh would be traded. The veteran is not a platoon-type bat and would be an everyday plug-and-play-type offensive piece in the middle of the lineup.
He won't be cheap.
Coming off one of his best seasons offensively, he will more than likely command a contract north of $100 million.
While not young either, the Phillies may not have a choice but to add another player in his 30s into the mix to capitalize on the closing title window.
Suzuki, who will turn 33 late next season, would bring similar traits to the lineup that Arozarena would, but perhaps on a more consistent level.
This season, he slashed .270/.368/.473 with an .841 OPS to go with 26 homers, 86 RBIs and a wRC+ of 134.
His 81 walks and 5.1 wins above replacement were career watermarks. It also marked a fourth consecutive season that he posted an OPS north of .800 and third in the last four years, where it was .840 or better.
The outfielder has been a consistent middle-of-the-order bat during his tenure with the Chicago Cubs.
Since 2023, he has had at least 140 hits, 27 doubles, 20 home runs and 70 RBIs. He would be two seasons removed from his best campaign of his five-year big league career in 2025, where he posted career-best in home runs (32) and RBIs (103).
His 113 career home runs are the third-most home runs in Cubs' history, only behind Kris Bryant (138) and Hall of Famer Ernie Banks (136).
During that same stretch he has averaged 28 homers and 97 RBIs per 162-game season. He also averages 72 walks per season during that span, and his patient approach would go a long way for a Phillies lineup that has repeatedly had chase issues, especially in the postseason when it’s become magnified.
Suzuki owns a slightly better career walk rate (10.9%) compared to Arozarena (9.8%).
He’s also a significantly better defender and made major improvements in that department this season. His 14 defensive runs saved this season were good for 17th-best among all outfielders, as opposed to Arozarena’s -2.
The other caveat with Suzuki is that he would be a different type of signing for the organization.
Philadelphia historically has not ventured into signing top Japanese talent, whether directly from Japan or even once they become assimilated stateside in MLB.
Of course, it’s not easy to break into such a market when there is no prior history. Add the fact that the Los Angeles Dodgers have established themselves as the premier destination for Japanese stars looking to take their talents to the top league in the world; it makes it all that more difficult.
The Phillies recently tried their luck with Koyo Aoyagi, a right-handed pitcher the team signed to a minor league contract before the 2025 season. Aoyagi posted a 7.22 ERA between Double-A and Triple-A and never made it to the big league club.
Other examples include Tadahito Iguchi, who they traded for in 2007 and So Taguchi, who they signed after spending six seasons with St. Louis. Neither was the caliber player Suzuki is and is not a success story that the team could use as a recruiting pitch to some of the top players, like star third baseman Teruaki Sato, who plays for the Hanshin Tigers of the Nippon Professional Baseball League.
General manager Preston Mattingly reportedly took a trip overseas to observe the 27-year-old who could be making his way over to the United States.
The Phillies also shouldn’t just sign Suzuki to say they signed a Japanese talent.
However, the talent is there and Suzuki would stabilize right field, a position that has become a revolving door over the last few seasons.
Like Arozarena, Suzuki would command a multi-year deal northwards of $100 million after he signed a five-year, $85 million deal with the Cubs.
But for a Phillies team that has spent years searching for stability in right field since Bryce Harper moved to first base, Suzuki wouldn't be simply another expensive bat. He'd be a proven middle-of-the-order hitter who gets on base, provides above-average defense, and has demonstrated the kind of year-to-year consistency the position has lacked.
Both players certainly fit the needs of the Phillies and wouldn't be a bad starting point to fix this roster.

item.content:encoded:
One thing that Boston Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow has shown multiple times since taking over the organization is that he's not afraid to make a splash in the trade market.
If you look at the Red Sox's 2026 roster, you'll notice a handful of guys were added by way of trade. Garrett Crochet, Sonny Gray, Erik Miller, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Curtis Mead, Andruw Monasterio, Caleb Durbin, Eli White and Willson Contreras, among others. The trade market has been Boston's avenue of choice to improve and nothing should be ruled out this winter. Sure, Boston's farm system isn't as good as it was a few years ago, in large part due to the trades, as well as promotions to the big leagues. But there are still plenty of pieces that could be used to bring talent to town this winter.
Arguably, the perfect fit would be Bryce Harper of the Philadelphia Phillies. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and USA Today's Bob Nightengale both have insinuated that Harper could be floated by the Phillies this offseason as a potential trade chip, if he is willing to waive his no-trade clause. We already have made the case for why he would be a great fit for Boston. But what could an actual trade look like? Here's a mock trade both sides should consider.
Red Sox Receive: OF/1B Bryce Harper
Phillies Receive: OF Jarren Duran, INF/OF Kristian Campbell, SP Tanner Houck
It's important to note that this is a mock trade. It's far more difficult to actually get a deal done, rather than talking about the idea. When it comes to Harper, the most important variables are whether the Phillies actually would be interested in trading the two-time MVP and then whether he would even be willing to waive his no-trade clause. If the answer to both of those questions was, "yes." Then, you could proceed.
The Phillies notably had a shaky outfield in 2026, plus Adolis Garcia is heading to free agency. Duran had a tough 2026 season, but this is also a guy who had 9.0 wins above replacement in 2024 and 4.9 wins above replacement in 2025. There are reasons to believe that he could get back to that level. Campbell would be the jewel of the deal. He's just 24 years old and already has a long-term deal. He could play in the outfield, or replace Luis Arraez in the infield.
When it comes to Houck, he's someone who is healthy now and who was an All-Star in his last full season in 2024. He got hurt in 2025 and missed all of the 2026 season, except the regular season finale. Still, he could either help in the rotation, or in the bullpen. Houck was selected in the first round of the MLB Draft in 2017, when Dave Dombrowski was still Boston's president of baseball operations.
Again, the idea of a Harper deal is a pipe dream right now. If the Phillies shop him and he is willing to waive his no-trade clause, then this could be more realistic. But there are also finances involved. He has five years left on his deal and will make just over $27 million in 2027 and 2028. Then, he'll make just over $23 million in each of the final three seasons. Are the Red Sox willing to take on that type of money? It would be better than spending something similar on Randy Arozarena or Seiya Suzuki.

item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Mariners seem likely to lose Randy Arozarena to free agency this offseason.
Those aren’t easy shoes to fill.
Arozarena has been a firm presence in the heart of the Mariners’ order for the past couple seasons. He also brings an energy and confidence that fires up the fans in the Pacific Northwest.
There really isn’t another guy quite like Arozarena out there, but if the Mariners are losing him, they have to at least consider what a replacement for him might look like.
The answer might not be out there in free agency. Instead, it might depend on Seattle’s pitching surplus to improve their roster on the hitting side of things.
Candidate to Replace Randy Arozarena
One candidate was suggested in a new article on Monday by Bleacher Report’s Kerry Miller.
The player: Emmanuel Rodriguez.
Rodriguez is a young outfielder who just made his debut for the Minnesota Twins this year.
“The Twins wouldn’t want to part with either Walker Jenkins or Kaelen Culpepper, but three guys a bit lower on their prospects list could be doable—with Emmanuel Rodriguez immediately becoming a candidate to fill the Randy Arozarena-sized hole in Seattle’s outfield,” Miller writes.
This is all in the context of Miller suggesting what he calls a “realistic” offseason trade for Mariners right-handed pitcher Logan Gilbert.
The package coming to Seattle would also including pitching prospect Riley Quick and infield prospect Ben Ross.
Rodriguez would be the centerpiece, though.
Rodriguez is 23 years old and originally from the Dominican Republic.
He’s been a top-100 prospect for each of the past four years in the rankings by Baseball America, MLB Pipeline and Baseball Prospectus.
Finally, he got to the bigs with the Twins at the end of the 2026 season. He went 8-for-45 (.178) with two doubles, a triple and two home runs. He actually had a 0.7 Wins Above Replacement in just 13 games thanks to a solid early impression with his defense.
The Mariners would have Rodriguez for the next half-decade if they made this deal, so it’d be worth considering.
Giving up Gilbert would be the tough part.
Case for Trading Logan Gilbert
If the Mariners were to trade Gilbert, it’d be because they have so much pitching depth.
He’s also entering the last year of his current contract.
“Between Emerson Hancock’s breakout, Kade Anderson’s arrival and Logan Gilbert’s projected salary of $16M in his final year of arbitration eligibility, the M’s might consider trading away the ace who was their Opening Day starter in both 2025 and 2026,” Miller writes. “At any rate, this starting rotation would still be quite formidable even without Gilbert. In addition to Hancock and Anderson, Seattle has George Kirby (through 2028), Bryan Woo (through 2029) and Bryce Miller (through 2029) for another two years. Ryan Sloan is also one of the top pitching prospects in all of baseball, and he might be a factor by the end of 2027.”
It’d be easiest to make this trade for Seattle if they can comprehend exactly what they’re getting in return. If they know they replace Arozarena’s spot in the lineup with an exciting young player, that certainly helps make the case for trading Gilbert.

Why Hyphen says Mariners need to ink Logan Gilbert to extension
Mariners analyst Ryan Rowland-Smith explains why keeping the right-hander is about more than just his performance.
(Olivia Vanni/Getty Images)
The Seattle Mariners have some heavy lifting to do this offseason as they attempt to bounce back from a disappointing 2026.
In addition to a managerial search, the Mariners have a few key players set to hit free agency, namely left fielder Randy Arozarena and longtime shortstop J.P. Crawford. And beyond those the soon-to-be free agents, they could also have an interesting decision to make with starting pitcher Logan Gilbert on the horizon.
Gilbert, who has a career 3.60 ERA and 1,089 strikeouts over 1,021 1/3 innings in six big-league seasons, will be in his final year of club control in 2027 and figures to be one of the biggest names to hit free agency after that season.
Seattle has yet to come to terms on any sort of contract extension with Gilbert, and reports of any extension talks between he and the M’s have been sparse.
So, with Gilbert entering his final year of club control with the possibility that he could leave afterwards, is he a trade candidate this offseason? Mariners analyst and former MLB pitcher Ryan Rowland-Smith doesn’t think that is a route the club should go with Gilbert. During Monday’s edition of Seattle Sports’ Wyman and Bob, Rowland-Smith explained why the M’s should lock down their talented right-hander with a new deal.
Rowland-Smith pointed to the way Gilbert pitched in what was a meaningless Game 162 for the M’s in their season finale as an example of why Gilbert needs to be retained.
“You got a dude who wants to pitch in (Game) 162, and the way he came out, it was not some wave to the fans and thank you. He (brought) the same intensity (he normally would),” Rowland-Smith said. “You need him when you’ve got a Kade Anderson, Ryan Sloan and so on to say, ‘This is how we do things.'”
In that final outing of the season, Gilbert struck out eight batters over four perfect innings before allowing a leadoff walk in the fifth that ended his day.
“Many guys would just say I don’t need to pitch… just have a bullpen day,” Rowland-Smith said. “Do you know how many guys I’ve played with who would do that? Do not get rid of Logan Gilbert – 1,000%.”
The 29-year-old Gilbert was one of just 13 pitchers to strike out 200 batters this season. He was also one of just five to do so while pitching at least 180 innings. The Stetson product has pitched at least 180 innings in four of his five full seasons in the majors, with the lone exception being in 2025 when he made the only trip to the injured list in his career.
“Pay the man. Have him here for a long time because he is so valuable,” Rowland-Smith said. “Logan Gilbert, sometimes I take him for granted. He’s, again, in the clubhouse and in that dugout, he is gold with some of these young players who you plan to bring up.”

item.content:encoded:
La trayectoria de Jonathan Aranda representa un recorrido destacado desde el beisbol infantil de Tijuana hasta los escenarios más importantes de las Grandes Ligas. El tijuanense pasó de formarse en los campos de la Liga Municipal de Tijuana a convertirse en pieza fundamental de los Tampa Bay Rays, equipo que aseguró su lugar en las Series Divisionales de los Playoffs de la MLB.
Durante la temporada regular 2026, Aranda tuvo un papel protagonista dentro de la ofensiva de Tampa Bay. El primera base e infielder mostró consistencia con el bate y terminó la campaña con un promedio de .277, además de sumar 156 imparables, 22 cuadrangulares y 92 carreras producidas, cifras que reflejan su importancia en el orden ofensivo de los Rays.
Su rendimiento fue determinante para que Tampa Bay alcanzara los playoffs con la mira puesta en avanzar a las siguientes rondas. Para Aranda, la clasificación representa otro paso importante en una carrera que comenzó en el beisbol tijuanense y que ahora lo coloca frente a uno de los mayores retos de su trayectoria. Aquí en Heraldo Deportes te contamos sus inicios y cómo llegó a Grandes Ligas.
Así fueron los humildes inicios de Jonathan Aranda en el beisbol de Tijuana
Jonathan Aranda encontró en el béisbol una oportunidad para mantenerse alejado de los entornos de violencia en Tijuana y construir un camino ligado al deporte. Nacido el 23 de mayo de 1998 en Baja California, comenzó a jugar desde pequeño con el respaldo de sus padres, Humberto Aranda y Ventura, quienes veían en esta actividad una forma de fomentar la disciplina y mantenerlo protegido. Con el paso de los años, aquella iniciativa familiar se convirtió en el inicio de una carrera que lo llevaría hasta las Grandes Ligas.
Durante su infancia, Aranda desarrolló su talento en las ligas infantiles y juveniles de Tijuana, donde destacó especialmente en la Liga Municipal. En esos campos también forjó una amistad con Alejandro Kirk, otro pelotero tijuanense que alcanzaría el máximo nivel del béisbol profesional. Ambos compartieron sus primeros pasos en el diamante y, con el tiempo, transformaron aquellos años de formación en una trayectoria que los llevaría a representar a México en la MLB.
Te puede interesar: Playoffs MLB 2026: Así puedes VER EN VIVO los juegos entre Yankees y Red Sox de Grandes Ligas
La historia de cómo Jonathan Aranda llegó a Grandes Ligas
El camino profesional de Jonathan Aranda comenzó con los Toros de Tijuana, donde fue identificado como uno de los jóvenes talentos de la región. El tijuanense pasó cerca de dos años dentro del sistema de desarrollo del club, trabajando principalmente en su capacidad de contacto y preparación ofensiva. En 2016 tuvo actividad con los Toros de Moroleón en la Liga Invernal Mexicana, una etapa que le permitió adquirir experiencia y llamar la atención de organizaciones de Grandes Ligas.
Su oportunidad con los Tampa Bay Rays surgió durante una sesión de visoría realizada en Tijuana en 2015. Los cazatalentos habían acudido para observar a Randy Arozarena, quien entrenaba con los Toros, y terminaron siguiendo de cerca el desempeño de Aranda. El bateador tijuanense convenció por su técnica y capacidad ofensiva, por lo que los Rays decidieron firmarlo por un bono de 130 mil dólares, dando inicio a su recorrido por las ligas menores. Siete años después, en 2022, Aranda debutó en la MLB y comenzó una nueva etapa de su carrera en el máximo nivel del béisbol.

Randy Arozarena se despidió de la afición de los Seattle Mariners durante el último juego de la temporada regular, y tras salir ovacionado, se alista para convertirse en agente libre para contratarse con otra organización de las Grandes Ligas.
El domingo 27 de septiembre de 2026, mientras se jugaba la séptima entrada del partido Mariners vs Angels en el T-Mobile Park, el pelotero cubano-mexicano a Randy Arozarena fue sustituido.
Arozarena fue acompañado camino a los vestidores por una emotiva ovación de pie y cánticos por parte de los aficionados de los Seattle Mariners.
El pelotero se quitó la gorra, saludó a las tribunas, cruzó los brazos en su icónica pose y abrazó a su compañero Julio Rodríguez.
El inminente adiós de Randy Arozarena a los Seattle Mariners
La despedida de Randy Arozarena de los aficionados de los Mariners sería más que un adiós a la temporada 2026 de las Grandes Ligas, representaría un cierre del ciclo con la franquicia de Seattle.
Cotizado por sus muy buenas temporadas en las Grandes Ligas, Randy Arozarena se convertirá en agente libre al finalizar la Serie Mundial del 2026, dejando su futuro en el aire para la temporada 2027.
La gran temporada de Randy Arozarena con Mariners antes de despedirse

Tras la emotiva ovación, ¿cuál será el destino de Randy Arozarena?
El seleccionado mexicano terminó la campaña con 26 jonrones, 26 robos y un OPS de .865, y ahora se prepara para entrar al mercado de agentes libres
El cierre de la temporada 2026 tuvo un significado especial para Randy Arozarena. En el último juego de los Seattle Mariners, frente a los Los Angeles Angels, el jardinero fue retirado en la séptima entrada y recibió una ovación de pie por parte de los aficionados en el T-Mobile Park.
Arozarena respondió al gesto quitándose la gorra y saludando a las tribunas. Después señaló el logotipo de los Mariners y volvió a levantar la mano para despedirse de los aficionados. Julio Rodríguez lo recibió con un abrazo antes de que abandonara el terreno, en una escena que rápidamente fue interpretada como una posible despedida.
La propia MLB difundió el momento y señaló que podía tratarse de la última aparición de Arozarena con el uniforme de Seattle.
UNA DESPEDIDA CON MUCHO SIGNIFICADO
La emotiva escena llegó justo cuando termina el contrato que Arozarena firmó con Seattle para 2026. El acuerdo fue por 15.65 millones de dólares y un año, y desde que se concretó quedó establecido que sería su última temporada antes de convertirse en agente libre.
El mexicano llegó a esta situación después de completar una de sus campañas más productivas con los Mariners. En 154 partidos, bateó para .281, conectó 26 jonrones, produjo 79 carreras, robó 26 bases y anotó 113 carreras, además de registrar un OPS de .865.
Su temporada también tuvo el reconocimiento de la Liga. Arozarena fue elegido All-Star por tercera ocasión en su carrera, después de haber sido seleccionado previamente en 2023 y 2025.
Uno de los datos que mejor explica la dimensión de su campaña es su regularidad. En agosto, Arozarena consiguió su sexta temporada consecutiva con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas.
Con ese registro ingresó a un grupo histórico de las Grandes Ligas junto con nombres como Barry Bonds, Bobby Bonds, Bobby Abreu y Willie Mays, quienes también consiguieron rachas de seis o más temporadas consecutivas dentro del club 20-20.
El logro tiene todavía mayor relevancia porque Arozarena lo consiguió combinando poder y velocidad durante seis campañas consecutivas, una característica que se ha convertido en una de las principales cartas de presentación del pelotero.
Arozarena llegó a los Mariners en julio de 2024, procedente de los Tampa Bay Rays, y rápidamente se convirtió en una de las figuras reconocibles de la organización.
Su primera temporada completa en Seattle, en 2025, terminó con 27 cuadrangulares y 31 robos, además de su segunda convocatoria al Juego de Estrellas. En 2026 volvió a ser seleccionado para el All-Star Game y terminó consolidando su producción con los números que consiguió durante la campaña.
La relación con la afición también se fortaleció a través de su particular personalidad y de sus celebraciones, pero sobre todo mediante una producción que lo convirtió en uno de los elementos ofensivos más constantes del equipo.
El cierre, sin embargo, llegó sin clasificación a la postemporada. Seattle terminó con marca de 76-86 y en el tercer lugar de la División Oeste de la Liga Americana, después de cerrar la campaña con una victoria de 7-3 sobre los Angels.
AHORA VIENE LA AGENCIA LIBRE
Con el final de la campaña también comienza una nueva etapa para Arozarena. Por primera vez en su carrera tendrá la posibilidad de negociar como agente libre, luego de concluir el contrato de un año que firmó con Seattle.
Su edad, producción y capacidad para combinar jonrones y robos serán algunos de los elementos que estarán sobre la mesa cuando los equipos comiencen a evaluar el mercado.
En Seattle, además, no será el único jugador importante que puede cambiar de uniforme. J.P. Crawford también quedó vinculado a la agencia libre, por lo que la organización tendrá que tomar decisiones importantes sobre varios integrantes de su roster.
Por ahora, cualquier versión sobre el próximo destino de Arozarena debe tomarse como especulación. No existe un acuerdo anunciado con otro equipo, y el mercado de agentes libres apenas comienza a tomar forma.
Lo que sí quedó definido fue su última imagen de 2026 en Seattle: Arozarena levantando la gorra ante un T-Mobile Park de pie y agradeciendo el cariño de los aficionados.
Después de dos temporadas completas con los Mariners, seis campañas consecutivas de 20-20 y una temporada 2026 con 26 cuadrangulares, 26 robos y un OPS de .865, el futuro de Arozarena queda ahora en manos del mercado. La ovación del domingo pudo ser un simple reconocimiento a su temporada o, efectivamente, el último adiós de Randy Arozarena como jugador de los Seattle Mariners.

item.content:encoded:
A common debate that I’ve had with league executives is how many $100+-million contracts will actually be handed out this winter.
Some say one. Others say two. Others say three. But what everyone can agree on is that this is a weaker-than-usual free agent class. The clear headliner is Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Tarik Skubal; after that, industry sources have a wide range of views as to how good this group is — and who should be considered the best non-Skubal target.
I've weighed in with my own take below. Here’s a look at the top 26 free agents of the coming winter, with educated guesses as to who will (and won't) opt out of their contracts in some cases.
1. LHP Tarik Skubal
Skubal is the consensus top free agent in the class, and the expectation is that just about all of the big-market teams will be bidding on the superstar left-hander. He should top the current record for a free-agent contract given to a starting pitcher, currently held by Yoshinobu Yamamoto at $325 million. One source predicted that Skubal could try to sign before the lockout to try and get ahead of CBA uncertainty, though his agent Scott Boras is known for waiting out the market.
2. OF Seiya Suzuki
Suzuki, 32, is one of the top bats on the market and has improved defensively in the corner outfield. He’s hit at least 20 home runs in four consecutive seasons, with a career-high 32 in 2025, and will have plenty of interest from offense-needy teams — with an early report already linking the slugger to the Toronto Blue Jays.
3. OF Randy Arozarena
Arozarena is Mr. Consistent. He’s posted six consecutive 20-20 seasons and he had a very strong contract year in 2026, hitting .281/.381/.484 with 26 home runs and 79 RBI. He’s earned a multi-year deal, one that eventually should top Teoscar Hernandez’s three-year, $66 million pact with the Dodgers.
4. 3B/OF Teruaki Sato (Hanshin Tigers)
Sato, 27, is hitting .315/.392/.620 with 37 home runs and 100 RBI this season in NPB. The third baseman/outfielder is the best power hitter on the market and is in the running to win the MVP award in Japan. It’s difficult to predict what he will ultimately sign for, especially after Munataki Murakami’s surprising free agency last year, but he will have a wide market of suitors.
5. LHP Trevor Rogers
Rogers, 28, has had an up-and-down tenure with the Orioles, from being traded to the franchise in 2024 to getting optioned to the Minors after posting a 7.11 ERA in four appearances. He then had a 1.81 ERA last season and has followed it up with a 4.03 ERA this year, though he once again finished strong with a 3.52 ERA in 79.1 innings in the second half.
6. RHP Freddy Peralta
It’s been a roller-coaster year for Peralta, who once seemed like a lock to sign a nine-figure contract but strugged enough with the Mets that a one-year deal seemed plausible, if not likely. Now, he’s bounced back with the Tampa Bay Rays, posting a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts, and one league source texted recently that he “will do just fine” in free agency. One additional note: Peralta is regarded as one of the best clubhouse guys in baseball. He is universally loved by every one of his teammates, past and present.
7. C Ryan Jeffers
At one point, Jeffers felt like a lock to be traded ahead of the Aug. 3 deadline, and he ultimately stayed with the Minnesota Twins. While he’s not the best defensive catcher in baseball, his offense more than makes up for it, and he hit .256/.353/.461 with an .814 OPS, 14 home runs and 56 RBI this season. With how many teams need catching, he seems primed to turn down the qualifying offer in favor of a multi-year deal this winter.
8. RHP Michael King
King is not technically a free agent, but we’ll put him here anyway. The 31-year-old has been tremendous for the Padres with a 3.21 ERA in 32 starts. There were concerns about his durability last winter, hence why he signed an opt out-heavy contract to return to San Diego (he had an in-division offer he strongly considered, too). And it should be noted that despite those concerns, his arm has relatively little wear and tear across eight Major League seasons (just 679.2 career innings).
9. 2B Brandon Lowe
I was talking on the phone with a high-ranking rival executive recently when Lowe’s name was brought up. “He’s a f***ing beast, bro.” He’s not wrong! Lowe hit 35 home runs with 96 RBI while slashing .260/.331/.493 in his first year in Pittsburgh. What’s been most noteworthy is his improvement defensively. He’s going to do very well in free agency, with plenty of teams eagerly awaiting the chance to sign the free-agent infielder.
10. LHP Adrian Morejon
Morejon was mentioned plenty at the trade deadline, but what was not mentioned much was that the Padres and A.J. Preller love the left-hander. They did not want to part with him and mess with their bullpen unless the offer was truly too good to pass up. A return to San Diego should not be ruled out. But a player with Morejon’s production (a 2.83 ERA in 76 appearances) while only being 27 years old will have an extensive market.
11. 2B Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Chisholm Jr. had a breakout season last year with the Yankees when he hit 31 home runs. His numbers have come down a bit in 2026, with the infielder hitting .231/.312/.399 with 19 home runs and 55 RBI. Still, he’s only 28 years old, younger than Suzuki and Arozarena, and has been to the postseason four years in a row. He’ll be one of the most talked-about free agents of the offseason, but the expectation I have from talking to folks across baseball is he’ll have a good market.
12. RHP David Bednar
For years, Bednar has been one of the best relievers in baseball. He was the subject of consistent trade interest with the Pirates, who ultimately traded him to the Yankees at the 2025 deadline. He’s been very good in the Bronx, with a 2.39 ERA in 86 games since being traded. He’s proven that he can pitch in the biggest of markets, which will only bolster his value. At only 31 years old, he’s primed for a lucrative multi-year contract.
13. OF Ian Happ
Happ, 31, has been one of the most consistent players in baseball across his 10-year career. He’s hit over 21 home runs in each of the last four seasons. His numbers this year declined, however, as he hit only .218/.326/.412 with 24 home runs and 68 RBI. He’s striking out more and his OPS+ finished at 103, noticeably lower than his career average of 114.
14. LHP Foster Griffin
Griffin was perhaps the steal of the offseason, with the Washington Nationals signing the left-hander for one year and $5.5 million. He posted a 3.06 ERA in 22 starts with the Nats and was eventually traded to the Guardians for multiple prospects at the deadline. He finished the year with a 3.60 ERA in 31 starts, and is in line for a multi-year contract this winter. He’s been a tremendous success story coming after coming back from pitching in Japan for three seasons.
15. 2B Luis Arraez
Arraez has always been one of the best hitters in baseball; his defense has been what has given teams hesitation. Those concerns are no more as he’s morphed into an above-average second baseman after working with Ron Washington in San Francisco. If healthy, he’ll have a real chance at a multi-year contract this offseason after slashing .310/.345/.419 with an .801 OPS.
16. RHP Sonny Gray
Gray is not technically a free agent, but he has a $30 million mutual option. Mutual options are never picked up, though, and if he becomes available, he will be heavily in demand — and a contract in the three-year, $75 million range would make plenty of sense. But he did recently tell Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com that he would retire “in a heartbeat” if his family indicated a desire for him to hang up his cleats. He clearly still has more in the tank, but this will be a situation to monitor that could affect the rest of the pitching market.
17. RHP Casey Mize
Mize, 29, appeared primed for a lucrative multi-year contract earlier this season when he had a 2.70 ERA in 16 starts with the Detroit Tigers. Since being traded to the San Diego Padres, he has a 7.46 ERA and a 25/19 strikeout-to-walk ratio. He could be a strong candidate for a short-term deal so he can have a better platform season and hit the market again after 2027 in hopes for a long-term contract.
18. LHP Robbie Ray
Ray, 34, is surely looking at a short-term contract at this stage of his career. He was consistent with the Giants, with a 3.54 ERA in 60 starts, but has struggled with the Padres to the tune of a 5.02 ERA (5.14 FIP). He’s proven durable the last couple seasons after missing significant time in 2023 and 2024 and can be a valuable innings-eater in the bottom half of the rotation. He won’t command top dollar, but any team who signs him will be very happy.
19. RHP Kevin Gausman
Parting with Gausman was very, very difficult for the Blue Jays. He’s been the model of consistency and durability, with the right-hander pitching at least 31 games in each season since 2021. His numbers declined this year, with a 4.51 ERA in 32 starts, though his 3.74 FIP paints a better picture. At 35 years old, he’s looking at a short-term contract. He’s still highly regarded in baseball circles and will have plenty of suitors.
20. RHP Clay Holmes
The amount of teams after Holmes at the trade deadline was massivem and had it not been for a failed physical involving a prospect, he would have been dealt to the Arizona Diamondbacks instead. He fits perfectly behind the Cubs’ elite infield defense, and considering that he is no longer eligible for the qualifying offer, his value has only increased. His market will once again be substantial.
21. OF Daulton Varsho
Varsho’s value comes with his defense in center field; he’s one of the best defenders in all of baseball. He showed growth offensively last season with the Blue Jays, with a career-high 121 OPS+. But he regressed this season, with a 76 OPS+ in 2026, including a 51 OPS+ in 41 games with the Houston Astros after being traded at the deadline.
22. INF JP Crawford
Crawford feels like a near-certainty to leave the Mariners in free agency. He’s been a mainstay in the infield the last eight seasons, with his best year coming in 2023 when he posted a 5.2 bWAR. His numbers dropped this season, as he slashed only .221/.335/.352 with a .687 OPS, 14 home runs and 40 RBI.
23. RHP Hiromi Itoh, Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters
Itoh, 29 in August, posted a 3.18 ERA in 172.2 innings. He has a seven-pitch arsenal and a fastball that touches 96 mph. He won the Sawamura Award in NPB, similar to the Cy Young Award, and teams have gotten a look at him in each of the last two World Baseball Classics.
24. RHP Dustin May
May, a former top prospect, has all the tools in his body. He has plenty of fans across baseball and there are some who believe he can still be a difference-maker atop a rotation — hence the Cardinals’ one year, $12.5 million contract for the right-hander in the offseason and the Milwaukee Brewers’ midseason trade for him. He’s since posted a 4.70 ERA in 31 starts, with a 3.63 FIP. A short-term contract once again feels likely for May.
25. OF Trent Grisham
Grisham, 29, accepted the qualifying offer last winter to stay with the Yankees for another season. While he broke out in 2025 with 34 home runs and 74 RBI, he came back down to earth with a .211/.308/.395 slash line with 18 home runs and 59 RBI this year. His 95 OPS+ puts him slightly below league-average this season. He feels like a candidate to once again sign a short-term deal in free agency.
26. 1B/OF Jake Bauers
Bauers has been a revelation in Milwaukee, and there is a real conversation to be had here about a potential qualifying offer. He’s hit .266/.389/.484 with 26 home runs and 86 RBI, and has emerged as a favorite of manager Pat Murphy, who recently noted that the slugger is being pitched to like one of the top hitters in baseball.
Honorable mentions: RHP Nick Martinez, C Carson Kelly, OF Taylor Ward, DH Joc Pederson, RHP Raisel Iglesias, OF/DH George Springer, RHP Jack Flaherty, RHP Tyler Mahle, LHP Kris Bubic,1B Ty France

item.content:encoded:
Contrary to popular opinion, the free agent market doesn’t consist of only one player. Yes, superstar starter Tarik Skubal will grab headlines since there’s nobody close. But while it may be seen as a one-man show, there are some other decent starters and useful position players. Here’s our top 30.
1. Skubal: MLB’s consensus top pitcher will almost surely beat Gerrit Cole’s $325M pitching record, which makes the Mets and incumbent Dodgers early favorites. He’s maintained his stuff following arthroscopic elbow surgery (“Skubal scope”) with a 2.95 L.A. ERA. It’ll be interesting if MLB’s salary cap desire affects things.
2. Bo Bichette,* INF: It’s certainly no guarantee he’ll opt out of $84M over two years (minus the unique $5M bonus for opting out) after an unremarkable year in Queens and yet another opt-out chance. But it’s a weaker free agent field, and the Phillies reportedly offered $200M over seven years last winter. They should have infield openings with Luis Arraez and Alec Bohm also free agents.
3. Randy Arozarena, OF: He timed his career year well, joining AL MVP Yordan Alvarez as the only players to post a 125 wRC+ every month, via MLB Network. Seattle needs Arozarena, whose clutch gene surfaced in the 2020 postseason.

Mariners rally past Astros 6-5 in 10 innings to keep faint playoff hopes alive
Posted/updated on: September 24, 2026 at 6:59 am
SEATTLE (AP) — Josh Naylor singled home Randy Arozarena with the winning run in the 10th inning and the Seattle Mariners kept their slim playoff hopes alive by rallying past the Houston Astros 6-5 on Wednesday night.
Houston (78-80) remained tied atop the AL West with Texas, which has lost three straight games. The Astros hold the head-to-head tiebreaker if the teams finish with the same record.
The Mariners (74-84) are four games back with four to play.
Seattle was down 5-4 after automatic runner Yordan Alvarez scored on a triple to right field by Isaac Paredes in the top of the 10th.
With one out and the bases loaded in the bottom half, Julio Rodríguez worked a full-count walk from Astros closer Josh Hader, forcing in J.P. Crawford with the tying run. Naylor sent Hader’s next pitch to right-center, and Arozarena scored his third run of the night.
Alvarez went 2 for 4 without an RBI in his pursuit of the AL Triple Crown. That raised his league-leading batting average to .316. Tampa Bay’s Chandler Simpson, second at .309, did not play Wednesday against the New York Yankees.
Alvarez is part of a four-way tie for the home run lead at 41 with the Rays’ Junior Caminero, Baltimore’s Pete Alonso and the Yankees’ Ben Rice. The Houston slugger is second in RBIs with 102, eight behind Alonso.
Before his tying walk, Rodríguez had three hits for the Mariners.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz and Nick Allen each had two hits for Houston. One of Diaz’s hits was his 14th homer, a two-run shot to cap a four-run third.
Cooper Criswell (4-2) pitched the 10th inning to earn the win for Seattle. Hader (4-2), who also pitched the ninth, took the loss.
Seattle scored three times in the third to pull to 4-3. The first two runs came on Dominic Canzone’s double as he extended his hitting streak to a career-best 12 games. Canzone’s single in the fifth scored Arozarena to tie it at 4.
Up next
The Mariners will send right-hander Bryan Woo (12-9, 3.92 ERA) to the mound Thursday in the opener of a season-ending four-game series against the Angels.
Right-hander Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.70) will pitch for the Astros in the first game of a four-game set at the Athletics.

Josh Naylor's walk-off single in 10th propels Mariners past Astros
(Photo credit: Joe Nicholson)
Josh Naylor lined a one-out single to center field with the bases loaded in the bottom of the 10th inning to score the deciding run as the Seattle Mariners kept their slim playoff hopes alive with a 6-5 victory against the visiting Houston Astros on Wednesday night.
Dominic Canzone drove in three runs for the Mariners (74-84), whose only chance to make the postseason is to finish in a three-way tie with Houston (78-80) and Texas (78-80), who are tied atop the American League West.
Yainer Diaz hit a tiebreaking triple in the top of the 10th inning after earlier hitting a two-run homer for the Astros.
Houston closer Josh Hader (4-2), who pitched the ninth, returned to the mound in the 10th to try and put the Astros into sole possession of the division lead. With J.P. Crawford the automatic runner, Hader walked Randy Arozarena before Canzone hit a slow roller to shortstop Nick Allen to advance both runners. A walk to Cal Raleigh loaded the bases and another to Julio Rodriguez forced in the tying run. Naylor lined the first pitch he saw from Hader up the middle to win it.
Mariners reliever Cooper Criswell (4-2) allowed one run on one hit with one strikeout in one inning.
The Astros opened the scoring with four runs in the top of the third off Mariners starter George Kirby. With one out, Allen doubled to left. Jose Altuve hit what turned out to be a single down the left-field line that deflected off third-base umpire Ryan Blakney's shin. Yordan Alvarez doubled to right, sending Altuve to third, before Isaac Paredes lifted a sacrifice fly to right. Diaz then lined a two-run shot over the left-field wall to make it 4-0.
The Mariners responded with three runs in the bottom of the inning against Astros starter Ethan Pecko. Lazaro Montes drew a leadoff walk and, an out later, Crawford grounded a single to right. Both runners advanced on a wild pitch. Arozarena walked to load the bases for Canzone, who lined a two-run single off the right-field wall. With two outs, Rodriguez lined a double to left to cut Houston's lead to 4-3.
The Mariners tied it in the fifth off reliever Josh Hendrickson, who was making his MLB debut. Arozarena lined a one-out single to center, stole second and scored on Canzone's single to center.
Pecko pitched 2 2/3 innings and gave up three runs on four hits. The rookie right-hander walked two and struck out two.
Kirby went five innings and allowed four runs on six hits. The right-hander walked three and fanned five.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Mariners were my World Series pick entering the year — that's how good I thought they'd be. Even if others weren't quite as high on them, there was every reason to believe this team could run away with a weak AL West. But that never came close to happening; in fact, just a year after making it to Game 7 of the ALCS, the Mariners will finish the 2026 campaign with a losing record and will miss the playoffs despite the American League being as weak as it's been at any point in recent memory.
Given how poorly this season went, major changes must be made to get this Mariners team back on track. Those changes begin with letting certain individuals depart after the year, starting with the most obvious one of all: manager Dan Wilson.
Manager Dan Wilson
Blaming the manager for things that have gone awry is often the easy way out, but what else can we do? On paper, the Mariners have one of the most loaded rosters in the sport, yet it feels like just about everyone has underperformed. Sure, a lot of the blame should be placed on the likes of Cal Raleigh, Julio Rodriguez, George Kirby and others who didn't do their jobs, but if everyone is failing to live up to expectations, there has to be something else going on, no?
Even if not, Wilson's lineup and bullpen management have been highly suspect dating back to his refusal to use Andres Munoz in the biggest moment of last year's ALCS decider. Wilson isn't the only reason why the Mariners are where they are, but he certainly hasn't helped them either. Again, major changes must be made, and the easiest move to start with would be letting Wilson go.
OF Taylor Ward
One move the Mariners tried to make to jumpstart their offense was trading for Taylor Ward, who, despite a down year in the power department, had an impressive .383 on-base percentage with the Baltimore Orioles prior to the trade deadline. Ward was drawing tons of walks and was essentially brought in as a table-setter for the likes of Randy Arozarena and Dominic Canzone. Unfortunately, Ward has been one of the worst hitters in the sport since the trade, going 9-for-85 (.106 BA) with one extra-base hit and no home runs. Ward's 15 wRC+ since the deadline ranks 269th out of 270 position players with at least 90 plate appearances in that span.
It's honestly a bit surprising that Ward hasn't been DFA'd to this point, but given the fact that he's a free agent after the year, it'd be stunning if Seattle even considered bringing him back. Sometimes, fits just don't work out as hoped, and this is one of those examples.
OF Victor Robles
Speaking of disappointing right-handed outfielders, what about Victor Robles? Not too long ago the Mariners had seemingly unlocked the best in Robles, who was one of their best players down the stretch of the 2024 campaign, but 2025 was a lost year for him, and 2026 went just as poorly.
Robles is slashing .256/.315/.308 with zero home runs in 65 games. Despite receiving 149 plate appearances, he has a grand total of five extra-base hits. Robles is still a decent defensive outfielder and offers a lot of speed, but he has a sub-.700 OPS against lefties and just hasn't hit enough to justify keeping around, even with one more year of club control.
SS/3B J.P. Crawford
J.P. Crawford is wrapping up his eighth season with the Mariners, and he's been a linchpin at the top of their lineup for most of those years. Crawford has always drawn a ton of walks, and his 13.3 percent walk rate this season places him in the 93rd percentile according to Baseball Savant. Unfortunately, Crawford doesn't hit for a very high average, doesn't hit for much power, doesn't offer much speed and is arguably the worst defensive shortstop in the sport.
For those reasons, is he really worth bringing back? Colt Emerson did struggle in his first taste of big-league action, but he was considered one of the best prospects in the sport and received a hefty pre-debut extension from the Mariners for a reason. He should be the shortstop on Opening Day 2027, and while Crawford could technically slide over to the hot corner, the team would benefit from finding an offensive upgrade at that position. Crawford was a great Mariner, but letting him walk in free agency feels like an easy choice.
RHP Bryce Miller
The Mariners considered trading either Bryce Miller or George Kirby at the trade deadline in their pursuit of adding a big bat to their lineup, and while they wound up settling on a rather Luis Castillo deal instead, there's no reason to believe talks won't heat up again this winter. At the end of the day, Seattle needs a game-changing bat, and they have a ton of pitching to offer up.
Logan Gilbert and Bryan Woo, their best starters, should be untouchable. The same goes for top prospect Kade Anderson. Kirby could get dealt, but his impeccable command makes him hard to part with. The Mariners could trade a Minor Leaguer like Ryan Sloan, but his upside is so massive that they'd probably shy away from doing so. That makes Miller, a pitcher with three more years of cheap club control and a very high ceiling, the likeliest choice to go. The Mariners shouldn't want to trade Miller, but given the free agent market's lack of high-end options and their starting pitching depth, a Miller trade for a middle-of-the-order bat makes too much sense.
OF Randy Arozarena
Randy Arozarena is one of the few Mariners players who actually surpassed expectations this season. He's slashing .279/.379/.480 with 26 home runs, 76 RBI and 24 stolen bases entering Wednesday's action. He's even scored an AL-leading 106 runs, which, given Seattle's brutal offense behind him, is pretty impressive. He's a player the Mariners should want back, but will he actually be back?
Arozarena is set to hit the open market this offseason, and with the kind of year he's had, he might be the best position player on the market. That reality will likely result in Arozarena receiving a ton of interest on the open market, and are we sure the Mariners will be outbidding teams in major markets? Letting Arozarena go would be an incredibly disappointing outcome, but the likely one nonetheless. The trade market is likely where they'll pursue their big bat.

Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 10:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Joe Nicholson)
Christian Walker hit a three-run home run, Yordan Alvarez launched a two-run homer and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot as the visiting Houston Astros slugged their way to a 7-0 victory over the Seattle Mariners on Tuesday.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz, Alvarez and Paredes each collected two hits for the Astros (78-79), who pulled into a first-place tie with the Texas Rangers in the American League West. Houston owns the head-to-head tiebreaker over Texas, so would win the division if the teams remain tied at the end of the season.
Five Astros pitchers combined to throw a four-hit shutout. Miguel Ullola (1-0) earned his first major league win, allowing one hit and striking out two over two innings.
Julio Rodriguez notched two hits for Seattle (73-84). The Mariners went 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and stranded nine.
Jeremy Pena led off the game with an infield single to shortstop, stole second, and scored on Alvarez's single to right. It marked the 100th RBI of the season for Alvarez, the second time in his career he's reached that milestone. Paredes and Altuve followed with singles, loading the bases with no outs.
Seattle starter Logan Gilbert (12-11) escaped the first-inning jam when Diaz struck out looking before Walker and Taylor Trammell flied out.
Altuve and Diaz opened the third with back-to-back singles before Walker launched his 26th home run of the season and the 200th of his career, a three-run shot to deep left, giving the Astros a 4-0 lead.
In the fifth, J.P. Crawford drew a one-out walk. After Randy Arozarena struck out swinging, Dominic Canzone singled to center. Crawford advanced to third, but Cal Raleigh struck out to end the inning.
Houston's advantage increased to 5-0 on Paredes' solo homer in the sixth.
With one out in the eighth, Pena was hit by a pitch, and Alvarez belted a slider over the wall in right for his 41st home run of the season, extending Houston's lead to 7-0.
Houston starter Cristian Javier tossed two shutout innings, allowing one hit and two walks while striking out two. The Astros announced Javier exited the game with groin tightness.
Gilbert gave up four runs on 10 hits over four innings, walking two and striking out three.
--Field Level Media

Mexicanos que ya aseguraron su pase a postemporada
La presencia de peloteros mexicanos en las últimas ediciones de los playoffs ha sido constante y este año no será la excepción pues hasta ahorita se tiene confirmada la participación de cuatro peloteros mexicanos y dos con estatus todavía pendiente, ya que uno está en sucursales y el otro se encuentra en lista de lesionados.
PUBLICIDAD
A continuación, te presentamos la lista de jugadores nacionales que estarán en los playoffs:

Ha firmado su campaña más sólida y consagratoria en MLB. Con 149 juegos jugados, el infielder presume un promedio de bateo de .277, conectando 156 imparables, 22 cuadrangulares y remolcando 92 carreras, convirtiéndose en una pieza medular en el lineup de los Rays.
Jarren Durán (Boston Red Sox):
Se ha consolidado como un auténtico motor en los senderos y el jardín central. A lo largo de la temporada suma 20 jonrones, 69 carreras impulsadas y 19 bases robadas en 145 encuentros, destacando además por su velocidad con 5 triples.

Ha sido una de las grandes revelaciones del año tras su llegada a Milwaukee, aportando una defensa de élite en el cuadro y un bateo sumamente oportuno que ayudó a los Brewers a amarrar temprano su boleto a octubre.
Patrick Sandoval (Boston Red Sox):
El lanzador que representó a México en el Clásico Mundial de Beisbol regresó esta temporada tras un periodo largo fuera de las canchas y ha tenido altibajos con los Boston Red Sox con una efectividad de 5.15 y un récord de 1-7.
Manuel Rodríguez (Tampa Bay Rays):
El lanzador yucateco venía sumando valiosos relevos con efectividad de 3.86 y 8 ponches en el bullpen de Tampa Bay en los cuatro juegos que disputó.

The Mariners can hope that Randy Arozarena stays. But they also know they need to prepare for what their 2027 lineup looks like without him. He has easily become one of the hardest bats to replace.
Seattle Times beat reporter Ryan Divish brought that problem into focus on Foul Territory. He expects Arozarena to prefer the East Coast and guessed Boston could be ready to pay him handsomely. It’s just a prediction. The Red Sox haven’t announced any kind of serious interest. Regardless of where he goes, the Mariners need to be prepared.
Randy Arozarena’s 2026 Surge Raises the Stakes for the Mariners
His first 54 games after the 2024 trade were uninspiring. He posted a .231 average, five home runs and a .733 OPS. In his first full Mariners season, he hit only .238, but supplied 27 homers and 31 steals. He kept producing even when the hits were harder to find.
This year, the whole line has changed. Entering Sept. 22, Arozarena is slashing .279/.376/.481 with 26 homers, 106 runs, 23 steals and an .857 OPS. Compared with 2025, his average is up 41 points, his OBP 42 points and his slugging 55 points. He has nearly matched last year’s career high in homers while reaching base more often.
Now put that beside Seattle’s .232/.312/.380 team batting line. Arozarena is 64 points ahead in OBP and 101 points ahead in slugging. If he walks, the Mariners lose a right-handed bat who gets aboard, hits for power and still runs.
What Arozarena Has Done at Fenway Park
Boston is easy to picture because Arozarena has already hit well at Fenway. In 32 career games there, he’s slashed .278/.351/.481 with five home runs and 19 RBI with a 135 wRC+ in those games, meaning his offense has been 35 percent above league average after adjusting for park. He also homered in consecutive games there during Seattle’s visit at the turn of September.
Thirty-two games cannot tell us what he would do over a full season with the Red Sox. The numbers do tell us he can handle that setting. His .481 career slugging percentage at Fenway even matches his .481 mark across this entire season. There’s no reason to sell a home run surge. But we can see the potential. Arozarena can turn on a pitch and drive it toward the Green Monster, where hard contact can become a double off the wall or a ball can fly over it. He has spent half his games trying to produce at T-Mobile Park. Fenway would be a much friendlier setting for half of his games. Also, being in the same division with the Yankees stadium could also help pile his stats.
The East Coast idea has a personal thread, too. Arozarena became a star with Tampa Bay and spent his last night as a Ray among the fans in Randy Land. We can wonder whether the Rays ever explore a reunion.
The Mariners should make Arozarena a serious offer. His age and below-average outfield grades give them a reason to be careful about the number of years. Divish doubts Seattle will chase Boston through a bidding war, and we understand why the club would set a limit. We will judge that limit alongside the plan for the lineup it leaves behind.
If Arozarena signs elsewhere, Seattle needs another proven bat and a credible answer in left field. The club should know which young players can compete for the job and what production it still has to acquire. Planning for life without Randy starts with admitting exactly how much Randy has given the Mariners.

He founded the Keep It Electric podcast in 2023 and covers baseball with a blend of analysis, context, and a little well-timed side-eye just to keep things honest. Tremayne grew up a Mariners fan in Richmond, Va., and that passion ultimately led him to move to Seattle to cover the team closely and become a regular at home games. Through his writing, he connects with fans who want a deeper, more personal understanding of the game. When he’s not at T-Mobile Park, he’s with his dog, gaming, or finding the next storyline worth digging into.

item.content:encoded:
Mientras marchamos por la última semana de la temporada regular, no parece haber mucho suspenso respecto a quiénes serán nombrados JMV. Al menos, eso es lo que podemos descifrar de nuestra más reciente -- y última -- encuesta del JMV de MLB.com para el 2026.
El cubano Yordan Álvarez sigue estando bien al frente en la Liga Americana a pesar de una producción relativamente mediocre recientemente. En la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong está cerrando una de las mejores campañas completas en tiempos recientes.
Treinta y ocho expertos de MLB.com emitieron sus votos sobre quiénes creen que se llevarán los honores de JMV tras esta temporada, con 32 jugadores recibiendo al menos un voto. Como recordatorio, los votos se basaron no solo en el desempeño hasta ahora, sino también en cómo se espera que evolucionen las cosas durante el resto de la campaña.
Los votantes clasificaron a sus cinco principales candidatos de cada liga con un sistema de 5-4-3-2-1: cinco puntos por un voto al primer lugar, cuatro por el segundo, y así sucesivamente. Estos son los resultados.
Todas las estadísticas son hasta la jornada del domingo, a menos que se indique lo contrario.
LIGA AMERICANA
Álvarez ha tenido un desempeño tan bueno este año que lo que califica como un bache para él sería un gran trecho para la mayoría de los demás bateadores. En sus últimos 41 encuentros, batea .264 con OPS de .840. Reiteramos, nada mal para la mayoría, pero muy por debajo del nivel del líder de la Americana en promedio (.313) y OPS (1.027). Álvarez lleva tres cuadrangulares y cinco impulsadas a lo largo de 16 partidos este mes, dejándolo a un jonrón del dominicano Junior Caminero de los Rays por el liderato en el Joven Circuito y a seis empujadas de Pete Alonso por la cima en dicho departamento. Aunque sus posibilidades de la Triple Corona se están desvaneciendo un poco, Álvarez todavía ha armado un 2026 asombroso en el plato. Su wRC+ de 179 es al menos 27 puntos mejor que el de cualquier otro bateador calificado.
Sabemos que el quisqueyano es uno de los grandes cañoneros del juego. Está cerrando su segunda temporada consecutiva de 40 vuelacercas y está dando swings más fuerte que nadie. Pero lo que ha sido más impresionante de su temporada es su mejorado criterio en la zona de strike. Aumentó su tasa de boletos desde un 6.3% por debajo del promedio a un 11.5%, lo que se ubica en el 80mo percentil de MLB. También ha mantenido una tasa de ponches muy sólida (18.5%). Ya no persigue tantos pitcheos fuera de la zona, ha reducido su tasa de swings en blanco y está haciendo más contacto en general. Esa mezcla de paciencia, trueno y control del bate es una combinación especial, sobre todo en un jugador de 23 años. Luciendo un porcentaje de embasarse de .363 (52 puntos mejor que la campaña pasada), el OPS de .892 de Caminero se ubica tercero en la Americana.
Witt ha tenido mejores campañas a la ofensiva, aunque 18 bambinazos, 43 estafadas y wRC+ de 119 en 137 partidos no está nada mal. Pero cuando se consideran todas sus capacidades, Witt sigue siendo extremadamente valioso. Su valor de carreras defensivas de +16 está empatado en el tercer lugar de las Grandes Ligas, y sus 22 outs por encima del promedio encabezan la Liga Americana. También cuenta con un valor de carreras en el corrido de bases de +8, a uno de Corbin Carroll de los Diamondbacks por el liderato de MLB. Por eso, aunque no ha sido tan indiscutible en la caja de bateo como lo fue en el 2024 (wRC+ de 169), la grandeza integral de Witt lo tiene en la cima de la tabla de posiciones de WAR de FanGraphs en el Joven Circuito (6.6) y posiblemente perfilándolo entre los primeros cinco en la votación para JMV por tercera vez en tres años.
Ha habido bastante conversación de JMV entorno a Schlittler en las últimas semanas. ¿Y por qué no? Está marcando el paso en la Americana en efectividad (1.94), WHIP (0.91) y WAR de pitcheo de FanGraphs (6.1). Se ubica segundo en el Joven Circuito en promedio de bateo en contra (.182) y en tasa de ponches menos boletos (25.0%). Ha permitido una carrera o ninguna en 21 aperturas. Ese es un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees y algo que apenas otros dos lanzadores de 25 años o menos han logrado en la Era de la Pelota Viva (desde 1920): Blake Snell (2018) y Dean Chance (1964). Seguramente será reconocido con el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana a estas alturas, pero Schlittler recibirá su merecida cuota de consideración para el JMV.
Schlittler no ha sido el único miembro de los Bombarderos que ha sido indispensable este año. Mientras Nueva York ha estado sin Aaron Judge durante una gran parte de la campaña y ha echado de menos a otros bates estelares debido a lesiones, Rice ha sido demostrado consistencia. Se ubica tercero en el Joven Circuito en jonrones (39) y anotadas (100). Es cuarto en la liga en impulsadas (95) y OPS (.888), y está empatado en el cuarto lugar en valor de carreras al bate (+34). Con dos vuelacercas durante la última semana, Rice se convertiría en apenas el segundo miembro del equipo del Bronx diferente a Judge en la última década en conectar al menos 41 jonrones en una temporada, acompañando al dominicano Juan Soto (2024).
Otros que recibieron votos: El venezolano Willson Contreras, Medias Rojas; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigres; el cubano Miguel Vargas, Medias Blancas; el cubano Randy Arozarena, Marineros; Munetaka Murakami, Medias Blancas; Dylan Cease, Azulejos.
LIGA NACIONAL
El mes pasado, PCA dio el salto por encima de Ohtani hacia el puesto Nro. 1 de nuestra encuesta. Este mes, se ha apartado por completo del resto del grupo. Crow-Armstrong, quien recibió cada voto de primer lugar emitido por nuestro panel, está empatado con Kyle Schwarber en el liderato de bambinazos de MLB (45). Nadie tiene más anotadas (118), extrabases (83) o total de bases anotadas (351) esta campaña. Con 38 estafadas, el dinámico jardinero central del equipo del Norte de Chicago podría convertirse en el séptimo miembro del club 40-40 más adelante esta semana. Y no pase por alto el hecho de que es posiblemente el mejor jugador a la defensa en cualquier posición en estos momentos. Ya no es una cuestión de si Crow-Armstrong es el JMV de la Nacional. El premio es prácticamente suyo ahora mismo. Pero ¿lo ganará de manera unánime?
Ohtani se mantiene como el claro escolta en el Viejo Circuito a pesar de haber jugado en apenas tres partidos este mes debido a sus persistentes lesiones en la rodilla izquierda y el bíceps derecho. La buena noticia es que el dirigente de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, dijo que "hay una buena posibilidad" de que Ohtani sea activado de la lista de lesionados de 15 días el miércoles tras cumplir la estadía mínima. No lanzará por el resto de la temporada, dejándolo con efectividad de 1.79 y 95 ponches en 85.2 entradas. Pero Ohtani tendrá unos cuantos partidos para sumar a sus totales ofensivos (30 jonrones, wRC+ de 142).
Mencionamos antes cómo Schlittler luce como el gran favorito para el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Misiorowski tendría su premio más asegurado en la Nacional. A lo largo de 169.1 episodios, Miz encabeza la Gran Carpa en casi cada categoría, incluyendo efectividad (1.86), WHIP (0.80), tasa de ponches menos boletos (31.7%) y fWAR (6.5), por nombrar solo algunas. Sus oponentes tienen un diminuto OPS de .474 contra Misiorowski, la segunda menor cifra para cualquier abridor calificado en la Era Divisional (desde 1969). Los oponentes del quisqueyano Pedro Martínez, en una de las mejores campañas para un lanzador, registraron OPS de .473 en el 2000.
El dominicano, quien no recibió un solo voto en nuestra anterior encuesta de JMV, ha estado encendido con Cincinnati durante el último mes. En sus últimos 27 encuentros, batea .404 con ocho vuelacercas, seis bases robadas y OPS de 1.205. Dio múltiples hits en 14 de esos partidos, y su fWAR de 2.5 durante este transcurso es el mejor de las Mayores. Esta prolongada racha encendida le ha dado a De la Cruz un wRC+ de 139 -- el mejor de su carrera -- y lo deja a dos jonrones más dos estafadas de convertirse en el cuarto jugador de los Rojos en el club 30-30 y el primero desde Brandon Phillips en el 2007.
Schwarber ha caído en un pequeño bache, bateando de 34-4 con un cuadrangular en sus últimos 10 encuentros. También está a ocho ponches de establecer un récord de ponches en una misma campaña. De todas maneras, hay que admirar la consistencia de Schwarber. Terminará con más de 40 vuelacercas y 150 juegos disputados en cuatro de las últimas cinco temporadas. Ha superado los 100 boletos negociados por cuarto año consecutivo, y un tercer título de bambinazos del Viejo Circuito está a su alcance.
Otros que recibieron votos: El dominicano Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Cerveceros; Matt Olson, Bravos; James Wood, Nacionales; Jordan Walker, Cardenales; Alex Bregman, Cachorros; Bryce Harper, Filis; Jake Bauers, Cerveceros; el dominicano Otto López, Marlins; el venezolano Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Rafael Devers, Gigantes; Alec Burleson, Cardenales; CJ Abrams, Nacionales; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; el dominicano Cristopher Sánchez, Filis.

As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll.
Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory.
Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they think will earn MVP honors after this season, with 32 players receiving at least one vote. As a reminder, votes were based not only on results so far, but also on how things are expected to play out the rest of the season.
Voters ranked their top five picks in each league on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on. Here are the results.
All stats are through Sunday unless otherwise noted.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Alvarez has been so good this year that what qualifies as a slump for him would be a good stretch for most other hitters. Over his past 41 games, he is hitting .264 with an .840 OPS. Again, not bad for most, but well below the standard of the AL leader in average (.313) and OPS (1.027). Alvarez has three homers and five RBIs through 16 games this month, leaving him tied with the O's Pete Alonso and one home run behind the Rays' Junior Caminero for the AL lead and nine RBIs behind Alonso for the top spot in that statistic. Even though his Triple Crown chances have faded, Alvarez has still put together an awesome 2026 at the plate. His 179 wRC+ is at least 27 points better than any other qualified hitter.
We know Caminero is one of the game's great sluggers. He is finishing up his second straight 40-homer season and swings harder than anyone. But what's been most impressive about his season is his improved strike-zone judgment. He has upped his walk rate from a below-average 6.3% to 11.5%, which ranks in the 80th percentile of MLB. He's also maintained a very solid strikeout rate (18.5%). He's not chasing as much, has shaved his whiff rate and is making more contact overall. That blend of patience, power and bat control is a special combination, especially in a 23-year-old player. Carrying a .363 on-base percentage (52 points better than last season), Caminero's .892 OPS ranks third in the AL.
Witt has had better offensive seasons, although 18 homers, 43 steals and a 119 wRC+ in 137 games is not too shabby. But when you consider his entire skill set, Witt remains extremely valuable. His +16 fielding run value is tied for third in the Majors, and his 22 outs above average tops the AL. He also has a +8 baserunning run value, one behind the D-backs' Corbin Carroll for the MLB lead. So while he hasn't been as undeniable in the batter's box as he was in 2024 (169 wRC+), Witt's all-around greatness has him atop the AL FanGraphs WAR leaderboard (6.6) and in line for a possible top-five finish in the MVP voting for the third time in three years.
There has been quite a bit of MVP chatter surrounding Schlittler in recent weeks. And why not? He is pacing the AL in ERA (1.94), WHIP (0.91) and FanGraphs pitching WAR (6.1). He ranks second in the junior circuit in opponents' batting average (.182) and strikeout-minus-walk rate (25.0%). He has allowed one or zero runs in 21 starts. That's a Yankees franchise record and something only two other pitchers age-25 or younger have accomplished in the Live Ball Era (since 1920): Blake Snell (2018) and Dean Chance (1964). He seems like a lock for the AL Cy Young Award at this point, but Schlittler will receive his fair share of MVP love.
Schlittler hasn't been the only indispensable Yankee this year. While New York has been without Aaron Judge for a large portion of the season and has missed other star bats as well due to injuries, Rice has been a constant. He ranks third in the AL in homers (39) and runs scored (100). He's fourth in the league in RBIs (95) and OPS (.888), and tied for fourth in batting run value (+34). With two homers during the final week, Rice would become just the second non-Judge Yankee over the past decade to hit at least 41 homers in a season, joining Juan Soto (2024).
Others receiving votes: Willson Contreras, Red Sox; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigers; Miguel Vargas, White Sox; Randy Arozarena, Mariners; Munetaka Murakami, White Sox; Dylan Cease, Blue Jays
NATIONAL LEAGUE
Last month, PCA jumped over Ohtani and into the No. 1 spot in our poll. This month, he has run away from the rest of the field. The recipient of every first-place vote cast by our panel, Crow-Armstrong is tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs (45). No one has more runs (118), extra-base hits (83) or total bases (351) this season. With 38 steals, the Cubs' dynamic center fielder could become the seventh member of the 40-40 club later this week. Oh, and let's not overlook the fact that he is arguably the best defensive player at any position right now. It's no longer a question of whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP. The award is as good as his right now. But will he win it in unanimous fashion?
Ohtani remains the clear runner-up in the NL despite playing in just three games this month due to his nagging left knee and right biceps injuries. The good news is Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said "there's a good chance" Ohtani will be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday after a minimum stint. He won't pitch for the rest of the season, leaving him with a 1.79 ERA and 95 K's over 85 2/3 innings. But Ohtani will have a few games to add to his offensive totals (30 homers, 142 wRC+).
We mentioned earlier how Schlittler looks like the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young Award. Misiorowski is an even bigger shoo-in in the senior circuit. Through 169 1/3 innings, Miz leads the Majors in just about every category, including ERA (1.86), WHIP (0.80), strikeout-minus-walk rate (31.7%) and fWAR (6.5), to name just a few. Opposing batters have a scant .474 OPS against Misiorowski, which is the second-lowest by any qualified starter in the Divisional Era (since 1969). Pedro Martinez, in one of the greatest seasons by a pitcher, recorded a .473 opponents' OPS in 2000.
De La Cruz, who didn't receive a single vote in our previous MVP poll, has been red-hot for Cincinnati over the past month. In his last 27 games, he is batting .404 with eight homers, six steals and a 1.205 OPS. He collected multiple hits in 14 of those games, and his 2.5 fWAR during this period is the best in the big leagues. This prolonged hot streak has given De La Cruz a career-best 139 wRC+ and has left him two homers and two steals away from becoming the fourth Red in the 30-30 club and the first since Brandon Phillips in 2007.
Schwarber has fallen into a bit of a rut, going 4-for-34 with one home run over his past 10 games. He's also eight strikeouts away from setting a new record for K's in a single season. Even so, you have to admire Schwarber's consistency. He will end up with more than 40 homers and 150 games played in four of the past five seasons. He has surpassed 100 walks for a fourth consecutive season, and a third NL home run title is right there for the taking, too.
Others receiving votes: Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Brewers; Matt Olson, Braves; James Wood, Nationals; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Alex Bregman, Cubs; Bryce Harper, Phillies; Jake Bauers, Brewers; Otto Lopez, Marlins; Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; Rafael Devers, Giants; Alec Burleson, Cardinals; CJ Abrams, Nationals; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies
